data.title: Tesla Begins Building Cybertrucks With 4680 Cells Using Lithium Refined in Texas
data.description:
Tesla has shared a new milestone in its Cybertruck program. The EV maker has started fitting the electric pickup trucks with 4680 battery cells made with lithium refined in Texas.

According to a Tesla X post, it has assembled the first Cybertruck powered by 4680 battery cells, based on output from the company’s lithium-refining facility in Texas on the Gulf Coast. This is a change from the company’s dependence on lithium imported from overseas, including China, Australia, and Chile.

Company CEO Elon Musk amplified the achievement by quoting the post with the words, “Lithium made in America.”

Tesla started construction of its refinery in Corpus Christi in May 2023 and has invested more than $1 billion. Operations started in 2024, but the refinery came fully online early in 2026, and production has since ramped up. The facility now sends processed lithium hydroxide to the Austin factory, where it is used to make 4680 cells. The Cybertruck production line is conveniently located within the Austin complex.

The Gulf Coast processing facility uses an alkaline leaching method to refine lithium, thereby reducing emissions by 30 percent. Another advantage of the process is that it slashes reagent costs by 60 percent. Tesla also profits from selling the anhydrite by-product as raw material for the construction industry. Bringing lithium refinery state-side insulates the automaker from the vagaries of the battery cell supply chain, which is notorious for steep price swings and associated geopolitical shenanigans.

Tesla already uses 4680 cells made in-house in the Cybertrucks. However, the latest update means the manufacturing process is now more vertically stacked. Tesla has not revealed plans to put the American-sourced battery packs in other models. The automaker has, however, raised Cybertruck prices in the US.

data.title: France Starts Testing Tesla FSD After Working With Elon Musk
data.description:
France has put two Tesla cars on the road to test the company’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) (FSD). The authorities are proceeding ahead of an upcoming EU vote on the advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS).

According to French Minister of Transport Philippe Tarabot, two Teslas equipped with FSD are now road-testing the autonomous technology. The update follows the steps of other European countries such as the Netherlands, which granted provisional approval this year. Belgium, Estonia, Lithuania, and Denmark also gave Tesla a partial go-ahead.

In Switzerland, Tesla started offering FSD ride-alongs last month. The drive sessions, in which a staff member sits behind the wheel, allow the public to experience ADAS first-hand. Similar programs exist in France, Germany, Italy, and Hungary.

Tarabot further stated that consultation with Tesla CEO Elon Musk about FSD paved the way for the test to begin. The minister also collaborated with Tesla staff to develop technical adaptations for French roads. This was a departure from Tarabot’s July position that the safety risks posed by FSD outweighed the potential benefits.

The transport ministry plans to conclude the two-vehicle test in September. The results will allow France to verify FSD data provided by Tesla.

The timeline is perfect as the EU vote on permitting FSD Europe-wide can take place as early as October. Tarabot, however, did not state whether France would support Tesla during the vote.

Tesla is preparing for the EU vote. The EV maker open-sourced FSD safety evidence that it shared with EU regulators this month.

data.title: NHTSA Opens Audit Into Tesla Cybercab’s Road-Legal Certification
data.description:
Tesla’s Cybercab has only just started carrying paying passengers in Austin, but federal regulators are already taking a closer look at how the company certified the two-seater was cleared for U.S. roads.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an audit on September 3, just hours after the first Cybercabs hit Austin streets as part of Tesla’s commercial Robotaxi service.

The issue isn’t a crash or a reported defect. Instead, NHTSA wants to know how Tesla certified the Cybercab as meeting federal safety rules when it has no steering wheel, pedals or traditional side mirrors.

Tesla says the Cybercab complies with all safety standards that apply to it. Now NHTSA wants to see the work behind that conclusion, including “the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues.”

One question regulators are looking at is whether Tesla determined that some Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) simply don’t apply to a vehicle designed from the start to drive itself.

U.S. rules are currently written around vehicles with a human driver. The Department of Transportation has proposed updating some of those requirements, including rules around brake pedals, but those changes aren’t finished yet.

The audit covers roughly 1,000 Cybercabs, although Tesla hasn’t put anywhere close to that number into service in Austin. As we reported earlier this week, Texas records showed 45 Cybercabs registered with the DMV.

An audit also doesn’t necessarily mean Tesla did anything wrong. Zoox went through a similar review before receiving an exemption in July that allows it to deploy up to 2,500 purpose-built autonomous vehicles per year for two years.

data.title: Starlink’s Memphis Discounts add over 2,000 New Customers
data.description:
As data center protests and complaints continue to circulate about new projects, Starlink’s localized 50% discount on its Residential Plan has added over 2,000 customers.

As we reported in June, SpaceX decided to slash Starlink monthly costs in half in response to growing community backlash over a nearby data center project.

The new updated numbers come from the SpaceXAI Memphis X account, which is providing updates on the Southaven data center project.

One of the major sticking points for the community and environmental law organization is that SpaceX is using a loophole in the current legislation to power the project. The company originally installed 69 portable gas turbines to power the data center, which did not require a permit.

However, in response to growing public anger over the unpermitted power plant, SpaceX confirmed they would replace all 69 portable units with 41 permanent turbines, which have been authorized under a Clean Air Act permit. However, this phase-out will take until July 2027 to be completed.

So, although some can enjoy heavily discounted Starlink services, the local pushback and potential legal action against the Southaven facility are not slowing down and could instead serve as a cautionary tale for tech companies looking to establish gas-powered data centers.

data.title: Tesla Cybercab Fleet Purchase Program Could Open Robotaxi Network to Third Parties
data.description:
Tesla is turning to the business community to gauge interest in buying Cybercab fleets or providing infrastructure for the Cybercab network.

The “Help Us Build Our Robotaxi Network” form, which launched on Tesla’s website ahead of the Cybercab Event in Austin yesterday, is collecting data on companies that are interested in:

  • Cybercab Fleet Purchase Program
  • Mobility Hubs and Infrastructure
  • Even Collaboration

This is an interesting wrinkle, as Tesla is playing catch-up with other robotaxi companies and seems to be looking to scale quickly with help from other companies.

There is no word on what a collaboration would look like, and Tesla provided no more details on its form. However, for those in the space, it suggests Tesla expects enough profit to share with third parties, rather than keeping it all in-house.

If Tesla moves in this direction, it would become the first robotaxi company to let third-party buyers purchase vehicles and the tech to run their own robotaxi fleet. All other companies are currently running their fleets in-house or in coordination with an established fleet management company, with no one announcing or hinting at selling to third parties. So, Tesla could be breaking new ground, which could be a great way to quickly play catch-up with Waymo.  

One thing still missing from Tesla’s plans is any indication of when individual customers will be able to buy a Cybercab. While the new form specifically mentions a Cybercab Fleet Purchase Program for businesses, Tesla has yet to announce a retail sales program, pricing, or a timeline for making the purpose-built autonomous vehicle available to the general public. However, Elon Musk did comment on a post from MKBHD (Marques Brownlee), who infamously has a bet that he will shave his head if Tesla offers a Cybercab to purchase for under $30,000 before the end of the year.

data.title: 2026 Tesla Model Y Earns IIHS Top Safety Pick+ With Perfect Crash Test Scores
data.description:
Tesla retains bragging rights as the Model Y earns the much-coveted Top Safety Pick+ designation. The electric SUV scored high across nearly all aspects of the crash test.

The refreshed 2026 Model Y (including 2027 builds) was rated Good in Small Overlap Front, Moderate Overlap Front, and Sides categories. It scored similarly under other tests, including Headlights, Front Crash Prevention (vehicle-on-vehicle), and Front Crash Prevention (vehicle-on-pedestrian).

The last two categories were achieved thanks to Tesla’s Automatic Emergency Braking system. However, the electric vehicle did not excel in seat-belt reminders, receiving a Marginal rating.

The Top Safety Pick+ ranking is organised by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS). The body awards Good (G), Acceptable (A), Marginal (M), and Poor (P) to vehicles for each of the tests, which are grouped into Crashworthiness, Crash Avoidance & Mitigation, Seat Belts & Child Restraints, Small Overlap Front, Driver-side, Passenger-side, Moderate Overlap Front, Side, and Others.

Tesla is no stranger to the top of the heap at the Top Safety Pick+ awards, as previous Model Y editions scored high, too. The 2026 Cybertruck also recently earned its own Top Safety Pick+ from the IIHS, making it the year’s safest pickup. The Model 3 sedan is another strong contender, having received similar high honors over multiple generations.

For context, the Kia Telluride earned the same accolades from the IIHS, though the automaker had to refresh the headlights on the 2027 model.

data.title: Tesla’s new Automatic Collision Evasion can turn on FSD to avoid a crash [2026.27.5]
data.description:
Tesla is preparing to roll out a new safety feature that can automatically turn on Full Self-Driving (FSD) when the vehicle determines the driver may not react to an imminent collision.

The new features is called Automatic Collision Evasion, and appears in release notes for software update 2026.27.5, which also includes FSD (Supervised) v14.3.9. The update has not yet been released to the public and is currently being tested internally by Tesla employees. We are unable to share the original screenshot of the release notes as it contains an employee’s VIN.

However, according to the release notes we were able to see, the feature is designed to engage while the vehicle is being driven manually. Importantly, since it is tied to FSD, it will only be available on cars with a FSD license or subscription.

“Automatic Collision Evasion activates Full Self-Driving (Supervised) to keep your vehicle safe and then continue driving. It can engage while you are driving manually and detects that you are not sufficiently attentive to the road (for example, reaching toward the back seat), or that Full Self-Driving (Supervised) may have been unintentionally disengaged.”

The description suggests the feature goes beyond Tesla’s existing Automatic Emergency Braking and collision avoidance systems. Rather than simply applying the brakes or making a short evasive steering manoeuvre, Automatic Collision Evasion can activate FSD to take control and continue driving after avoiding the immediate danger.

Tesla also appears to be combining information from its exterior cameras with the cabin camera. The latter is already used for driver monitoring and can determine where the driver is looking, allowing the vehicle to recognize situations where the person behind the wheel may not be paying enough attention to respond.

Another notable part of the release notes is that Automatic Collision Evasion can intervene if FSD was unintentionally disengaged. Tesla doesn’t provide further details on what circumstances would qualify as an accidental disengagement.

The release notes also say owners should check the owner’s manual for more information, but the manuals have not yet been updated to include this new feature.

For now, the feature looks like it will be included with FSD v14.3.9 in software update 2026.27.5. As with any Tesla software release, wider public availability is unknown and if bugs are found during internal testing, its release could be delayed and not included in FSD v14.3.9.

data.title: Tesla Robotaxi fleet surpasses 1 million miles of unsupervised driving
data.description:
Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet has now surpassed 1 million miles (1.61 million km) of unsupervised driving, a major increase from the figure the company disclosed less than two months ago.

In its Q2 2026 update in July, Tesla said its fleet had accumulated more than 380,000 miles (about 612,000 km) of unsupervised operation. At the time, the figure drew considerable criticism as it came roughly a year after Tesla first launched its Robotaxi service, and about six months after it began fully autonomous operations.

Many also compared it to Waymo’s autonomous mileage count at over 200 million miles.

However, during Tesla’s Cybercab launch event in Austin on Thursday, Tesla’s head of AI, Ashok Elluswamy, revealed their figure has now jumped to more than 1 million miles (1.6 million km).

“As a testament to the safety I am happy to announce that we have achieved 1 million miles of unsupervised robo taxi operation,” Elluswamy said during the presentation.

The milestone means Tesla has added roughly 620,000 miles, or nearly 1 million kilometres, since the previous announcement in July. The cumulative total has increased by approximately 163%, reaching more than 2.6 times the earlier figure.

The company didn’t provide a city-by-city breakdown of its 1 million unsupervised miles, nor how much of the total was accumulated with Cybercab testing. Tesla currently operates driverless robotaxis in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Tampa, Miami, and Orlando.

With 1 million miles under their belt, that number should start climbing even faster for Tesla. Cybercab officially joined the Robotaxi fleet to select riders on Thursday, and Tesla says public Cybercab rides in Austin will begin Friday at 5 p.m. CT.

data.title: Tesla Reveals New Cybercab Details As It Officially Joins Robotaxi Fleet at 5pm Tonight
data.description:
Tesla held its Cybercab launch event in Austin yesterday, and while the company didn’t livestream the presentation, they did reveal lots of new details about the purpose-built robotaxi – everything from its efficiency and manufacturing process to the passenger experience.

One of the biggest new specifications is Cybercab’s aerodynamics. Tesla says the two-seater has a drag coefficient below 0.20, making it one of the most aerodynamic production vehicles ever developed. The company deliberately designed it for two passengers, saying more than 80% of rides involve two people or fewer.

Tesla also provided more details about what happens before a Cybercab even arrives. The Robotaxi network will search for nearby vehicles, including those currently completing another trip, and select whichever can reach the passenger fastest. Dynamic pricing will be used to balance supply and demand.

Once assigned, Cybercab will begin loading preferences stored in the rider’s Tesla account, automatically adjusting the temperature and seat position and restoring media accounts. A unique colour on the front light bar and interior lighting will help passengers identify their ride, while the Robotaxi app will display a compass pointing toward the correct vehicle.

Grok is integrated into Cybercab as well, accessible by voice, touchscreen or the app, with control over certain vehicle and ride functions. Tesla described the cabin as a “second living room” where passengers can watch videos, listen to music or work during a trip.

Accessibility was another major focus. Cybercab includes Braille on its doors and pull-over buttons, while the large butterfly doors provide a wider opening for passengers entering and exiting the vehicle. Tesla says it worked with disability groups and first responders during development.

Tesla also showed off Cybercab’s new Unboxed manufacturing process, which assembles separate vehicle modules rather than moving a completed body through a traditional production line. Tesla says the process reduces line size by 50% while allowing substantially higher output. The exterior panels use an injection-moulding process and recycled materials, eliminating the need for a conventional paint shop.

The event also brought a major milestone for Tesla’s broader autonomous program, with the company announcing its Robotaxi fleet has now accumulated more than 1 million miles of unsupervised driving.

Cybercab officially joined that fleet Thursday night to those who attended the event, and the next step won’t take long. Tesla says Cybercab rides will open to the public in Austin on Friday at 5 p.m. CT., although they didn’t specify how many Cybercabs will be available.

As we told you earlier this week, the company registered 45 units with the Texas DMV, so the fleet will likely only be that size, unless more are registered on Friday.

data.title: Another day, another Tesla driver ticketed for allegedly sleeping behind the wheel in B.C.
data.description:
If this story sounds familiar, it should. But no, this isn’t déjà vu. Yesterday we told you about how a Tesla driver had been fined for allegedly sleeping behind the wheel on Highway 1 in North Vancouver.

Today, police have released video of yet another incident. This time it happened on August 27 at around 7:45 a.m., during the morning rush hour on Highway 1 near 248 Street in Langley.

According to B.C. Highway Patrol, an officer was travelling to a priority call when he passed a Tesla and noticed the man behind the wheel with his eyes closed and both hands off the steering wheel.

The officer diverted from the original call and pulled the Tesla over.

“The police officer’s observations and his Body Worn Camera appeared to show the Tesla driver was asleep, though the driver claimed otherwise,” said Sergeant Michael McLaughlin with BC Highway Patrol. “This traffic stop took a valuable resource away from another police call. If drivers would stop sleeping behind the wheel, we could go help people who need us more.”

The driver was handed a $368 ticket for driving without due care and attention, along with an $81 fine for failing to produce a driver’s licence.

Other officers were ultimately able to respond to the original call, which involved a man with an extensive police history walking on the highway.

This is now the fifth separate incident involving an allegedly inattentive Tesla driver reported in B.C. this year.

In March, a Model Y driver was ticketed after allegedly appearing asleep on Highway 1 in Coquitlam. A West Kelowna driver was then caught reading documents while using Full Self-Driving (FSD) in July. That same month, another driver was filmed apparently asleep between Golden and Revelstoke.

Then on Wednesday, police revealed a fourth incident in which witnesses recorded a Tesla driver allegedly asleep on Highway 1 in North Vancouver on August 11.

Not to sound like a broken record, but Tesla’s FSD (and Autopilot) is a Level 2 driver-assistance system. Regardless of how capable the technology may be, the driver remains responsible for staying awake, attentive and ready to take control.
